## The project in one slide

::: {.nonincremental}
- **Teams of four.** You form them today.
- **Pick a track.** Visit a research group (Track A) or take your own measurements (Track B).
- **Do it first-hand.** Over the next four weeks.
- **Teach the class.** A 15-minute presentation on Nov. 6 or Nov. 13.
:::

::: {.highlight-box}
You can't do this project from your desk. The evidence of what you did (your photos, your data, your conversations) is the core of your talk.
:::

::: notes
Full details are on the Team Project page: ../assignments/team-project.qmd. This project supports the
course learning outcome on leading and participating in collaborative projects. It also previews the
undergraduate research lecture on Nov. 20.
:::

---

## Why do this as a team?

Physics is a team sport.

::: {.nonincremental}
- Research groups divide work: someone builds, someone analyzes, someone writes, someone talks to collaborators.
- Most of the hard problems in a group project are **people** problems: who does what, when you meet, what happens when someone goes quiet.
- You will practice solving those now, when the stakes are 25% of a one-credit course.
:::

## Part I: The two tracks {.section-slide background-color="#003057"}

## Track A: Inside a Physics Lab

Find a research group, visit, and interview the people who do the work.

::: {.nonincremental}
- **Where:** School of Physics preferred. Elsewhere is fine if the work relates to physics.
- **Experimental group:** tour the lab; watch a measurement if you can.
- **Theory or computation:** attend a **research group meeting** instead.
- **Interview** the PI and, if possible, a grad student or undergraduate researcher.
:::

::: {.highlight-box}
**Finding a group is your team's job.** Start emailing this week; professors can take a week to reply.
:::

::: notes
Groups outside the School of Physics need a short explanation of the physics connection in the
contract, and my approval. The talk covers the research question, how the group answers it, the
people and their paths, and how a first-year can get involved.
:::

---

## Finding a group

::: {.nonincremental}
1. Browse the [School of Physics research pages](https://physics.gatech.edu/research) and faculty profiles.
2. Look at recent seminar and colloquium speakers on the [events calendar](https://physics.gatech.edu/events).
3. Ask upper-year students, your Team Leader, and the professors teaching your classes.
4. Pick a first choice and **one or two backups**. All of them go in your contract.
5. Before you email, read the group's website and one accessible article, news story, or talk.
:::

::: notes
The Physics\@Tech talks on Oct. 16, 23, and 30 (tentative) are also a way to meet faculty.
Encourage teams to spread out across research areas so the four presentations are not all on the
same topic.
:::

---

## Writing the email

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
::: {style="font-size: 0.7em; border: 1px solid #B3A369; padding: 0.6em 0.9em;"}
**Subject:** GT 1000 first-years: request to visit your lab

Dear Professor Lastname,

We are four first-year Physics majors in GT 1000. For a class project, we would like to learn how your group studies *[topic]*. We read *[article or news story]* and were curious about *[one specific thing]*.

Could we visit the lab (or sit in on a group meeting) and interview you for about 30 minutes? We are free *[two or three times]* between Oct. 12 and Oct. 30.

Thank you for considering it,<br>
*[Names]*
:::
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
::: {.nonincremental}
- **Short.** Fits on a phone screen.
- **Specific.** Shows you read something.
- **Easy to say yes to.** Clear ask, clear times.
- **Professional.** GT email, no slang.
- **Follow up** politely after about a week.
- **Thank them** within a day or two of the visit.
:::
:::
::::

::: notes
This is the same skill as emailing a professor about undergraduate research later. Point out that
the Liaison sends the email but the whole team should read it first.
:::

## Track B: Measure Tech

Measure one physical quantity **two independent ways**, then compare.

| Experiment | Method 1 | Method 2 |
|---|---|---|
| Height of Tech Tower (or Howey) | Phone barometer, bottom vs. top | Shadows and trigonometry, or a pendulum |
| Local *g* | Long pendulum in a stairwell | Timed drop with an acoustic stopwatch |
| Radius of the Earth | "Two sunsets": ground, then up a tall building | Angle of the horizon from a rooftop |
| Speed of sound | Echo off a large building wall | Two phones over a measured distance |

Or propose your own in your contract. Free phone apps such as [phyphox](https://phyphox.org/) turn your phone into a lab instrument [@staacks2018].

::: notes
Apparatus can be built at the Montgomery Machining Mall or the Invention Studio. Safety: public
spaces only, follow building rules for roofs and stairwells, never drop anything where people walk.
:::

---

## Example: how tall is Tech Tower?

Air pressure drops as you go up, because there is less air above you:

$$\Delta P = \rho_{\text{air}} \, g \, \Delta h \quad\Rightarrow\quad \Delta h = \frac{\Delta P}{\rho_{\text{air}} \, g}$$

With $\rho_{\text{air}} \approx 1.2~\text{kg/m}^3$, that is about **12 Pa (0.12 hPa) per meter**. Phone barometers can resolve changes this small.

::: {.nonincremental}
- Repeat the measurement several times. How much do the results scatter?
- What else changes the pressure while you walk up the stairs? (Weather? Air conditioning?)
- Then measure the height a **second, independent** way and compare.
:::

::: notes
1.2 kg/m^3 times 9.8 m/s^2 is about 11.8 Pa per meter. Air density depends on temperature and
humidity, which is a good source-of-error discussion. Don't give the actual height of the tower;
that's what they're measuring.
:::

---

## Do your two methods agree?

Report each result as a value with an uncertainty: $h = 30 \pm 2~\text{m}$.

::: {.nonincremental}
- **Uncertainty** comes from repeating the measurement and looking at the spread, and from the limits of your instruments.
- Two results **agree** if their difference is about the size of their combined uncertainty or smaller.
- If they **don't** agree, that is not a failure. It is the most interesting part of your talk: what did one method miss?
:::

::: {.highlight-box}
A careful "our methods disagree, and here is why" beats a suspiciously perfect match.
:::

::: notes
The 30 +/- 2 m is a made-up example of the format, not the real height. Rule of thumb for the
"combined uncertainty": add the two uncertainties in quadrature. They will see this formally in
PHYS 2211/2231 lab.
:::

## Part II: How it gets graded {.section-slide background-color="#003057"}

---

## Roles

Every member has a primary role, and **every member presents**.

| Track A: Inside a Physics Lab | Track B: Measure Tech |
|---|---|
| **Liaison** &mdash; outreach, scheduling, thank-you note | **Project Manager** &mdash; schedule, internal deadlines |
| **Interview Lead** &mdash; prepares and leads the questions | **Lead Experimentalist** &mdash; designs and runs measurements |
| **Science Lead** &mdash; background; explains the physics | **Data Analyst** &mdash; uncertainties, plots, comparison |
| **Media and Deck Lead** &mdash; photos, slides | **Communications Lead** &mdash; photos, video, slides |

::: {.highlight-box}
Roles divide the work. They do not excuse anyone from the rest of it.
:::

---

## Evidence of your work

::: {.nonincremental}
1. **Your own dated photos or video** of your team doing the work. Ask before photographing people or equipment in a lab.
2. **A signed Verification Form:** from your lab host (Track A), or from the Team Leader after watching one data-collection session (Track B). It goes on the last slide.
3. **A check-in with the Team Leader by Oct. 23:** photos, notes or raw data, and progress against your contract.
:::

::: {.highlight-box}
Generative AI is strongly discouraged in this course, and it can't visit a lab or take your data. Anything you present as your experience must actually be your experience.
:::

::: notes
Track B teams: schedule the observed session with Elouan early; one Team Leader, several teams.
The Verification Form is still being written; it will be posted on the Team Project page.
:::

---

## The presentation

::: {.nonincremental}
- **15 minutes:** about 12 minutes talking, 3 minutes of questions. We will keep time.
- **Everyone presents,** roughly equally. Plan the hand-offs.
- **Questions** can go to any team member about any part of the project.
- **10&ndash;15 content slides,** plus title, references, and the Verification Form.
- **All slides are due Nov. 6,** even if you present on Nov. 13.
:::

| Slides (100) | Presentation (100) |
|---|---|
| Content 30 &middot; Evidence 30 &middot; Organization 15 &middot; Design 15 &middot; Sources 10 | Delivery 30 &middot; Teamwork 20 &middot; Questions 20 &middot; Timing 15 &middot; Check-in 15 |

## Part III: Working as a team {.section-slide background-color="#003057"}

---

## What strong teams do

From the GT 1000 textbook [@gt1000_group]:

::: {.nonincremental}
- **Meet in person** to plan, at least once.
- **Assign clear roles,** and check everyone is comfortable with theirs.
- **Keep talking** between meetings (GroupMe, Teams).
- **Rehearse together,** out loud, so hand-offs are smooth and gaps show up.
- **Give each other specific feedback.** You share the grade.
- **Have a backup plan** for a dead laptop or a sick teammate.
- **Raise problems early.** If someone goes quiet, talk to them, then to the Team Leader or me **before** the deadline.
:::
